headline: Open-Source Video Generation Arrives, and the Training Data Question Follows
lede: A clip generated by LTX 2.3, an open-source video model capable of running on consumer hardware, has prompted both admiration and a familiar suspicion: that the impressive output is partly a function of training on content its creators had no right to use. The observation is not new, but seeing it arrive in a locally-runnable, freely distributed package sharpens the stakes. One commenter's aside — "probably not just books" — neatly connects the video debate to the still-unresolved legal battles over how large language models were trained.
body:
LTX Video is an open-source video generation model. Version 2.3, referenced here, apparently runs without cloud infrastructure — a capability that until recently was associated only with well-funded labs. The original poster's astonishment ('when did open source video models get this good?') is a reasonable response: the quality gap between proprietary and freely available systems has been closing faster than most forecasts anticipated.

The training data question is the real subject of both posts. @RoyalCities writes that 'it's not hard to guess what it's trained on,' a reference to the widespread assumption that high-quality video generators are trained on copyrighted film, television, and user-uploaded video — material gathered at scale without explicit license. No research sources were available to confirm LTX 2.3's specific training corpus, so that assumption remains unverified here.

@MagisFuturum extends the point beyond video. 'This isn't ChatGPT but it probably is not just books' draws a line between the book-scraping allegations that have dogged large language models — the subject of multiple ongoing lawsuits from publishers and authors — and the analogous situation in video. The implication is that **questionable training data provenance is a structural feature of frontier AI, not an exception**. That argument has gained traction in court filings even if it hasn't yet produced a landmark ruling.

The aside about Sora is worth treating carefully. OpenAI's *Sora* — its text-to-video system, unveiled in early 2024 — has had a turbulent and limited rollout, but describing it as 'shut down' appears to overstate matters; no definitive shutdown has been confirmed in publicly available reporting as of this writing. The sentiment that open-source models have undercut the commercial case for a cautious proprietary rollout is plausible, but the framing elides the difference between 'struggling to scale' and 'shut down.'

concepts.definition: AI models that convert text (or other inputs) into short video clips and whose weights and code are released publicly, allowing anyone to run them without paying a cloud provider. The practical threshold — whether a model can run on a consumer GPU rather than a data-center cluster — matters enormously for adoption and distribution.

The origin and licensing status of the material used to teach an AI model. Provenance questions arise because models trained on large internet scrapes or pirated media may reproduce copyrighted work or were built using data the copyright holders never consented to share. Several lawsuits against AI companies hinge on this point.

Running an AI model entirely on a user's own hardware — laptop, desktop, or workstation — rather than sending requests to a remote server. Local inference means no usage fees, no data sent to a third party, and no dependency on a company's continued operation or access policies.

fact_check: The claim that 'Sora got shut down' appears to be an overstatement. OpenAI's Sora had a limited and troubled rollout after its February 2024 demonstration — including capacity problems and restricted access — but no public announcement of a full shutdown has been confirmed. The more defensible reading is that Sora has underperformed commercially relative to expectations, not that it ceased to exist. No research sources were available to verify LTX 2.3's specific training data, so the implied claim about its corpus cannot be confirmed or denied here.
